**_Procedures:_** Let _S ⊆ X_ be a neural safe set that is, in the avoid case, the _complement_ of the neural reachable tube being verified. In our case, _S_ is typically a super- _δ_ level set of the learned value function _V_<sup>˜</sup> ( _x,_ 0). Ideally, any super- _δ_ level set of _V_<sup>˜</sup> ( _x,_ 0) for _δ >_ 0 should be a valid safe set; however, due to learning errors, that might not be true in practice. To provide a probabilistic safety assurance for _S_ , we first sample _N_ independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) states _x_ 1: _N_ from _S_ according to some probability distribution P over _S_ . Since _S_ is defined implicitly by _V_<sup>˜</sup> ( _x,_ 0), we use rejection sampling. All proofs can be found in the Appendix of the extended version of this article<sup>1</sup> . Disregarding the confidence parameter _β_ for a moment, Theorem 2 states that the fraction of _S_ that is unsafe is bounded above by the violation parameter _ϵ_ , where _ϵ_ is computed empirically using Equation (2) based on the outlier rate _k_ encountered within _N_ samples. _ϵ_ is thus a reflection of the safety quality of _S_ , which degrades with the increase in the number of outliers _k_ , as expected. This can also be seen for the running example in Figure 1 (the red curve). Overall, Theorem 2 allows us to compute probabilistic safety guarantees for any neural set _S_ based on a finite number of samples. Subsequently, this result can be used to find some _S_ for which _ϵ_ is smaller than a desired threshold, as we discuss later in this section.

To interpret _β_ , note that _k_ is a random variable that depends on the randomly sampled _x_ 1: _N_ . It may be the case that we just happen to draw an unrepresentative sample, in which case the _ϵ_ bound does not hold. _β_ controls the probability of this adverse event happening, which regards the correctness of the probabilistic safety guarantee in Equation (3). Fortunately, _β_ goes to 0 exponentially with _N_ , so _β_ can be chosen to be an extremely small value, such as 10<sup>_−_16</sup> , when we sample large _N_ . 1 _− β_ will then be so close to 1 that it does not have any practical importance.

We have just explained the robust scenario-based probabilistic safety verification method in the case where _L_ represents undesirable states. When the system instead wants to reach _L_ , _S_ will be a sublevel set instead of a superlevel set of the learned value function. The cost inequality should be flipped when computing _k_ , and the value inequality should be flipped in Equation (3).
